title: Modi Just Met Myanmar's Military Ruler in New Delhi. The West Wanted India to Isolate Him.
excerpt: Min Aung Hlaing's first visit to India since becoming president drew sharp criticism from human rights groups. India said engagement works better than isolation. The 1,643-km border is the reason.
body:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks with Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing in New Delhi on Monday — a meeting that drew immediate criticism from Western governments and human rights organisations but underscored India's determination to chart its own course in its immediate neighbourhood.

Min Aung Hlaing, the former army chief who seized power in a 2021 coup that toppled the elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, arrived in India on Saturday. He first visited Bodh Gaya in Bihar — the Buddhist pilgrimage site where the Buddha is believed to have attained enlightenment — before heading to the capital for formal talks at Hyderabad House.

## Why India Won't Isolate Myanmar

Indian Foreign Minister Vikram Misri was direct in his defence of the meeting. "We have always assumed that sustained dialogue is what is important," Misri told reporters. "History has shown that disengagement does not get us better results than engagement."

Misri added that Indian policy "is not intended to be a commentary on the internal political arrangements" in Myanmar — a carefully worded rejection of the Western approach of imposing sanctions and cutting off diplomatic contact.

India shares a 1,643-kilometre border with Myanmar, stretching across the northeastern states of Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram. For New Delhi, Myanmar is not an abstract human rights case — it is a security reality. Cross-border insurgent movements, drug trafficking, and refugee flows directly affect India's northeastern frontier.

## The Western Backlash

Western countries have sought to isolate Myanmar's military rulers since the 2021 coup, which triggered a brutal crackdown on pro-democracy protesters and sparked a civil war that has displaced millions. The United States and the European Union have imposed successive rounds of sanctions on Myanmar's military leadership.

Human rights groups criticised Min Aung Hlaing's visit to India, saying it risks conferring legitimacy on a regime accused of widespread atrocities. The military government has been accused of air strikes on civilian areas, arbitrary detention, and the systematic suppression of dissent.

But India has consistently declined to join Western sanctions regimes against its neighbours, maintaining that its geographic proximity and strategic interests require a different approach.

## What Was Discussed

The official readout from Hyderabad House was sparse, but diplomatic sources indicated the talks covered border management, counterinsurgency cooperation, the ongoing civil conflict in Myanmar's border regions, and India's infrastructure projects in the country — including the long-delayed India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project.

India has invested heavily in connectivity projects that would give its landlocked northeastern states access to Southeast Asian markets through Myanmar. The civil war has stalled much of this work, making engagement with whoever controls Myanmar's government a practical necessity.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For Indian-Americans watching from abroad, Modi's meeting with Min Aung Hlaing fits a pattern: India's willingness to engage with regimes that the West has written off. New Delhi has maintained ties with Russia through the Ukraine war, held talks with the Taliban in Afghanistan, and now extended a red carpet to Myanmar's military president.

The approach reflects India's view of itself as a civilisational power that maintains relationships across ideological lines — a posture that sometimes puts it at odds with the values-based foreign policy framework favoured by Washington and Brussels, but one that Modi's government has shown no inclination to abandon.

This is the first visit by Min Aung Hlaing to India since he was sworn in as president in April following an election widely criticised as aimed at consolidating military rule. His previous visit was in 2019, when he was still Myanmar's commander-in-chief.

**Sources:** Al Jazeera, Reuters, Indian Ministry of External Affairs, Associated Press
author: Diaspora Desk
